Using the Planetary Spectrum Generator for radiative transfer modeling and employing the previously predicted vertical distribution proposed by V. Vuitton et al., E. Lellouch et al., J. C. Loison et al., and V. A. Krasnopolsky, we derived the upper limit column density of HC 5 N, corresponding to 3 σ noise level, to be 0.3–10 × 10 13 molecules cm –2 above ∼60 km altitude (depending on the assumed vertical profile).

Using models other than those of V. Vuitton et al. (2019), we obtained a lower upper limit for the [HC 5 N]/[HC 3 N] ratio, with a value of 0.04–0.17, which is lower than that found in protostellar objects.

For the case of V. Vuitton et al. (2019), by considering the HC 5 N abundance only above 60 km, where HC 3 N is present (M. A. Cordiner et al. 2014), the [HC 5 N]/[HC 3 N] ratio is newly derived as <0.43.
Similarly, HC 5 N column density and [HC 5 N]/[HC 3 N] from V. A. Krasnopolsky (2009) changes to 0.3 × 10 13 molecules cm –2 and 0.012, respectively.
For comparison with their result, we have used a similar kind of the vertical profile (twolayer model) and obtained the upper limit as 13% of A. Marten et al. (2002).

Our abundance upper limit of 5.2 × 10 −11 above 60 km is 8 times lower than the previously published upper limit for this species, which demonstrates the power of ALMA for searching for new molecules on Titan.
Integrating six independent observation data sets with a total integration time of ∼15,000 s, we found no statistically significant detection of an HC 5 N spectral feature.

The nondetection of HC 5 N is found to be consistent with the photochemical model profile from J. C. Loison et al. (2015) and V. Vuitton et al. (2019), but not with the model of both E. Lellouch et al. (2010b) and V. A. Krasnopolsky (2009)—the latter models significantly overestimates the atmospheric HC 5 N column density.

The corresponding upper limit of [HC 5 N]/[HC 3 N] ratio value derived from three of four models seem to be lower than that measured in high-mass protostellar objects, possibly due to the lower abundance of C 4 H 2 .

The relatively low [HC 5 N]/[HC 3 N] ratio we found implies that synthesis of progressively longer carbon chains is less efficient on Titan than in the cold interstellar medium and protostellar envelopes.

As stated in their paper, note that such a twolayer model is unlikely, and the slope-like vertical distribution is a more appropriate description.
